summary: Specifies Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode, a multicast routing protocol that can use underlying unicast routing information. It builds unidirectional shared trees rooted at a Rendezvous Point for each group, and optionally shortest-path trees per source. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 7761.

plainLanguage.summary: PIM-SM lets routers deliver one multicast stream to multiple receivers without sending a separate copy from the source to every receiver. Routers first build a shared path through a Rendezvous Point, and may later use a more direct path from a source.

subtitle: How multicast routers build shared and source-specific trees to deliver traffic to interested receivers.

tldr.problem: Multicast senders and receivers may not know about each other in advance, so routers need to build delivery paths only where receivers request traffic.
tldr.mechanism: PIM-SM builds a shared tree through a Rendezvous Point, then can build source-specific paths and prune traffic from the shared tree.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4601 was obsoleted by RFC 7761 and also updated by RFCs 5059, 5796 and 6226.

today: RFC 4601 has been obsoleted by RFC 7761. It was also updated by RFC 5059, RFC 5796 and RFC 6226.

sections.title: What PIM-SM Does
sections.content:
Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) routes multicast groups across wide-area networks. It can use unicast routing information or a separate multicast routing information base (MRIB), but does not depend on a particular unicast routing protocol.

The MRIB tells a router which neighbor lies on the reverse path toward a destination. PIM uses that information to direct Join and Prune messages; data then follows the paths created by those messages.
sections.plainLanguage: PIM-SM builds delivery paths for multicast traffic when receivers express interest. It uses routing information to choose where routers send requests to join or leave those paths.

sections.title: Building the Shared Tree
sections.content:
A receiver's local router, called its Designated Router (DR), learns that the receiver wants a multicast group, typically through IGMP or MLD. The DR sends a (*,G) Join toward the group's Rendezvous Point (RP), and routers along the path create state for group G.

Joins from receivers converge at the RP to form a shared tree. A sender's DR encapsulates the sender's packets in unicast Register messages to the RP. The RP decapsulates them and forwards them down the shared tree, where routers replicate packets at branches.
sections.plainLanguage: Receivers' routers send Join messages toward a meeting-point router called the RP. A sender's router sends traffic to that point, and routers copy it only where the shared delivery tree branches.

sections.title: Moving Traffic onto Shorter Paths
sections.content:
Register encapsulation can add processing work and may send packets on a detour through the RP. The RP can respond by sending an (S,G) Join toward source S. When native packets arrive, the RP drops the encapsulated copies and sends Register-Stop to the source's DR.

A router near a receiver may also choose to join a source-specific shortest-path tree. Once packets arrive on that path, it prunes the source's traffic from the shared tree, so the receiver gets traffic along the more direct route.
sections.plainLanguage: The RP can ask routers to send a source's packets along a native path instead of inside Register messages. A receiver's router can also join a direct path to the source and stop taking duplicate traffic from the shared tree.

sections.title: Hello Messages and the Designated Router
sections.content:
PIM routers send Hello messages periodically on every active PIM interface to discover neighbors, elect a DR and negotiate options. The RFC requires Hello messages on point-to-point links as well as LANs. The IPv4 and IPv6 all-router groups are 224.0.0.13 and ff02::d.

The DR acts for directly connected hosts. A priority option can influence the election; the default priority is 1. A generation identifier is a randomly generated 32-bit value that changes when PIM forwarding restarts, helping neighbors detect a restart.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers announce themselves to nearby PIM routers with Hello messages. They elect one DR on each interface to handle PIM actions for directly connected hosts.

sections.title: Forged Messages and Protection
sections.content:
Forged PIM messages can waste bandwidth, disrupt a Designated Router's role or stop multicast traffic from reaching a LAN. Forged Register messages can also inject traffic at an RP, while forged Register-Stop messages can prevent a source's DR from registering packets.

The RFC recommends IPsec Authentication Header for message integrity and origin authentication, with anti-replay enabled. It also describes denial-of-service risks that message authentication does not prevent, including many requests to different multicast groups.
sections.plainLanguage: A forged router message can change which traffic reaches a network or consume router resources. IPsec authentication can help verify PIM messages, though the RFC notes that it cannot prevent every denial-of-service attack.
